summary: Defines a way to store named IMAP searches persistently on the server and then use them in a SEARCH or any other command that takes a search criterion. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: If you often look for the same kind of email, save the search under a name. Next time, just use the name.

subtitle: Save a favorite IMAP search on the server under a name, then reuse it by name in later searches.

tldr.problem: Email clients often repeat the same long searches, and resending the full criteria each time wastes bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The FILTERS extension stores a search criterion as a server annotation under a name, and adds a FILTER search key that the server replaces with the stored criterion.
tldr.outcome: Clients can save, share and reuse named searches using the existing SETMETADATA and GETMETADATA commands. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Search key
facts.value: FILTER followed by a filter name

today: RFC 5466 is a Proposed Standard from February 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the METADATA extension in RFC 5464.

sections.title: Saved Searches on the Server
sections.content:
RFC 5466 defines a way to persistently store named searches (called filters) on an IMAP server. A saved search can then be used in a SEARCH command, or in any other command that takes a search criterion. The RFC says this can save bandwidth for clients that regularly repeat the same searches.

A server supports the feature when it advertises the FILTERS capability. The extension adds a new FILTER search criterion for referencing a filter, and it reuses the GETMETADATA and SETMETADATA commands from the METADATA extension (RFC 5464) to list, create, update and delete filters. The base protocol is IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501).
sections.eli5: The server keeps a notebook of your favorite searches. Each one has a name, so you do not have to write the whole thing out again.

sections.title: Private and Public Filters
sections.content:
A filter can be private (only the logged-in user can reach it) or public (all logged-in users can). A private and a public filter with the same name can exist at the same time. The RFC calls a pair of filter name and filter type a typed filter.

Each typed filter has a value, which must be a valid IMAP search criterion, and an optional human-readable description. If both a private and a public filter share a name, the FILTER search key MUST use the private one. Otherwise it uses whichever one exists. All search keys stored in a filter MUST be encoded in UTF-8.
sections.eli5: You can keep a search just for yourself, or put it on a shared shelf for everyone. If both shelves have a note with the same name, yours wins.

sections.title: The FILTER Search Key
sections.content:
The syntax is FILTER <filter_name>. When the named filter exists, the server inserts its stored criterion verbatim in place of the FILTER key. In the RFC's example, a filter named on-the-road holds OR SMALLER 5000 FROM "boss@example.com", so the search with UID 300:900 FILTER on-the-road and a SINCE key behaves as if the stored text had been typed in place.

A reference to a filter that does not exist, or that the user cannot access, MUST make the SEARCH fail with a tagged NO response carrying the UNDEFINED-FILTER response code and the filter name. The server SHOULD also check that each stored criterion is complete and correct. A stored OR SMALLER is missing a parameter, so a search that uses it should fail.

A filter can itself use FILTER. Implementations MUST be able to perform at least 3 substitution passes. If an implementation allows more passes it MUST detect loops. If it detects a loop, or still sees a FILTER key after at least 3 substitutions, it MUST behave as if the filter does not exist.

Using FILTER implies the CHARSET "UTF-8" parameter. If the command gives an explicit charset other than UTF-8 or US-ASCII, the server MUST answer with a tagged BAD response containing the BADCHARSET response code.
sections.eli5: Saying a filter's name is like saying 'the usual' at a cafe. The server swaps in the full order. If there is no such usual, it tells you so.

sections.title: Managing Filters with METADATA
sections.content:
A compliant server MUST either implement the METADATA-SERVER (or METADATA) extension, or implement SETMETADATA and GETMETADATA so they work with an empty mailbox name (server annotations) and for the entries this RFC defines. The RFC reserves these entry roots: /private/filters/values and /shared/filters/values for the search criteria, and /private/filters/descriptions and /shared/filters/descriptions for descriptions.

  • Create or change: store a non-NIL value in the filter's values entry with SETMETADATA. The server SHOULD verify the criterion is complete.
  • Delete: store the NIL value in both the private and the shared entry.
  • Rename: create a filter with the new name and the same value, then delete the old one.
  • Too many filters: if the server's maximum is reached it MUST return a tagged NO with the [METADATA TOOMANY] response code.

Filter names are limited to a subset of US-ASCII and may not be meaningful to people, so descriptions are stored separately in UTF-8. A private description is used first, then a shared one, and with neither the client MAY show the filter name. Descriptions SHOULD carry language tags, and the i-default language is assumed if there are none.

Because several clients may edit the same filter, a client storing a search key not defined in RFC 3501 SHOULD wrap it in parentheses, so that other clients can partly parse the value.
sections.eli5: You add, change or throw away a saved search by writing on or erasing the note in the server's notebook. Each note can also have a friendly label so people know what it is for.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The grammar is written in ABNF. It adds FILTERS as a capability, adds FILTER SP filter-name as a search key, and adds UNDEFINED-FILTER SP filter-name as a response text code. A filter-name is one or more atom characters except /. That excludes UTF-8 and the characters (, ), {, space, %, the asterisk and ]. Servers MUST accept the keyword strings case-insensitively.
sections.eli5: The rules for names are strict: plain simple characters only, so every computer reads them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general issues of IMAP SEARCH and of the METADATA extension apply. The RFC adds two specific warnings.

First, heavy use of filters can make denial-of-service attacks easier, especially with poor implementations that lack loop detection. Servers that allow anonymous access SHOULD NOT let anonymous users create, edit or delete filters.

Second, stored filters can reveal personal information. When confidentiality matters, clients MUST use TLS and/or a SASL security layer. Clients should also prefer private filters over public ones unless they want to share the information.
sections.eli5: Saved searches can show what you care about, so keep them private unless you want to share. And a note that points to itself in circles could keep the server busy forever, so servers must spot that.

data.title: A FILTER key and its expansion
data.code:
C: a SEARCH UID 300:900 FILTER on-the-road SINCE "3-Dec-2002"

is equivalent to:

C: a SEARCH UID 300:900 OR SMALLER 5000 FROM "boss@example.com"
   SINCE "3-Dec-2002"
